newsitem.title: USA: Ontario Hydro to meet U.S. power users over supply.
newsitem.headline: Ontario Hydro to meet U.S. power users over supply.

text.p: Ontario Hydro officials will meet with U.S. customers next week to discuss their power supply arrangements for 1998 when seven of its nuclear power units will be shut for extensive overhaul.
"We'll be meeting with U.S. customers next week to insure their needs are met," Ontario Hydro spokesman John Fox said.

On Wednesday, the provincially-owned utility announced the temporary shutdown of those units for upgrade and massive overhaul of its beleaguered nuclear operations, an undertaking which could cost between C$5 billion ($3.6 billion) and C$8 billion ($5.8 billion) over five years, starting in 1997.
U.S. customers have been assured their contractual supply will not be disrupted despite that 4,400 megawatts (MW) of Ontario Hydro's generating capacity will be laid up next year.
"They told us, 'It (contractual supply) will not be impacted by this decision'" a spokeswoman for Consumers Energy Co, a subsidiary of CMS Energy Co said.
Consumers Energy and Detroit Edison Co, an affiliate of DTE Energy Co, have a 600 MW firm power agreement with Ontario Hydro that continues through 2001.
Through its transmission connections, the Michigan utilities could import up to 2,200 MW of energy from Ontario.
Ontario Hydro has not finalized the steps it will take to meet its supply commitments with U.S. customers.
"We're just exploring the various options in how their needs will be met," Fox said.
Those options include buying power from other suppliers and restructuring the terms of the contracts, he noted.
Ontario Hydro planned to close its four 500 MW Pickering A nuclear power units at the end of December and three 800 MW Bruce A units at the end of March 1998.

The electricity generated by the seven nuclear units will be replaced by operating existing fossil-fuel plants at Nanticoke and Lambton at higher levels and bringing back two mothballed oil-fired units.
Nanticoke's eight units have a total generating capacity of 4,000 MW, while Lambton's four units have a total capacity of 2,000 MW.
Two 500 MW units at the Lennox generating station will be reactivated.
